prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of GLP-1 physiology and the development of incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: I opened with imatinib in first place, but the opening ballots show that five of six members place GLP-1 first, and their arguments are scientifically sound rather than merely numerous. GLP-1 offers the most complete chain from hormone physiology (Holst on secretion and action in humans, Drucker on proglucagon-derived peptide biology) to drugs (long-acting analogues) with large randomized outcome trials showing benefit in diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular and renal disease. The discovery is original, mechanistically clear, independently replicated for decades and of exceptional public-health impact. On the same criteria imatinib remains very strong, but its upstream discovery (Philadelphia chromosome, BCR-ABL) lies outside the credited trio and the prize was already recognized by the Lasker in 2009, while GLP-1 combines mechanism and medicine in a single, currently dominant story. I therefore move GLP-1 to the top of my own preferred configuration, keeping the physiology-to-drug span with Holst, Drucker and Knudsen.
statement.case_against: Credit allocation is the weak point. Mojsov (identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide) and Habener-type early peptide work have real claims, and I cannot verify priority independently from the supplied record. Choosing Knudsen over Mojsov privileges drug development over peptide discovery, and a prize that blends physiology and an industrial development program risks being read as rewarding a product. The alternative physiology-only trio would omit the person who delivered the durable drugs. Any three-name set leaves out defensible contributors.

responses.point: Perlmann proposes Drucker, Holst and Mojsov as the most defensible trio, treating Knudsen's liraglutide and semaglutide development as an industrial contribution.
responses.response: I take the Mojsov argument seriously, since identifying the truncated active peptide is a discovery step and not only chemistry. I still weigh the long-acting analogue work more heavily, because without it the incretin hormone would not have become a drug; the clinical impact the committee cites for ranking this first depends on that step. I would not treat the choice as settled, and I could accept Mojsov in place of Knudsen if the committee decides the citation should be confined to discovery. The disagreement is about the citation's scope, not about the importance of the field.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranks GLP-1 first and also places B032 (unfolded protein response, Walter and Mori) fourth as a clean, mature basic discovery that stands without clinical translation, and supports June and Sadelain only for CAR-T.
responses.response: I agree that the unfolded protein response is a conceptually clean two-person discovery with fully mature evidence, and I would not hold its limited clinical output against it. My reservation is that, unlike GLP-1, its disease relevance is inferred from many different settings rather than demonstrated by a therapy, so I rank it below the candidates with proven medical outcomes this year. I also agree that restricting CAR-T to June and Sadelain avoids the weakest link in Rosenberg's adjacent work, but then the original chimeric-receptor concept is still unrepresented, and that unfairness persists.

responses.point: Svenningsson, as chair, ranks optogenetics (B043) second and accepts the compound credit among Nagel, Hegemann, Bamberg, Boyden, Deisseroth and Miesenbock as a real difficulty, while noting limited clinical translation.
responses.response: As a circuit neuroscientist I know how much causal dissection optogenetics has enabled, and I ranked it third, so I will not discount it. But I think it should be judged as a tool, and for that reason it does not need to displace a medicine discovery with proven patient benefit; I would not accept my own field's familiarity with the tool as a reason to move it up. Your point about Miesenbock's earlier genetically targeted photostimulation reinforces my view that the three-name limit makes this the hardest attribution on the list, which is why I keep it as an alternative rather than my preference.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranks optogenetics second and describes recognition as overdue, and ranks imatinib last (eighth) on her ballot while noting upstream BCR-ABL discoveries.
responses.response: I disagree with placing imatinib that low. Its upstream discoverers do complicate the story, but the demonstration that inhibiting a driver kinase controls a cancer, with over two decades of survival data, is exactly the sort of proof of concept the prize has honored before. I accept that it may be read as drug development rather than discovery, which is why I now put GLP-1 above it. On optogenetics I partly agree with you on maturity, but I do not think a method alone is overdue in the same sense as a therapy that has changed disease outcomes.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks GLP-1 first with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, and notes that Habener's absence and Knudsen's industrial peptide engineering make credit disputed; he ranks the SMA antisense work (B047) sixth.
responses.response: Your caution about Habener and the primary-discovery chronology is the same uncertainty I have, and neither of us can resolve it from the supplied evidence. On B047, I place it fifth and find the mechanism-to-drug link clear, but I agree that its being placed behind the better-established candidates is reasonable, given its more recent approval and the competing SMA therapies.

uncertainties: Whether the citation should honor GLP-1 physiology and discovery only (Mojsov in) or span to drug development (Knudsen in).
Priority between Mojsov and Habener-type early GLP-1 work, which cannot be verified from the supplied record.
Whether the committee will treat imatinib as already recognized through upstream discoveries and the Lasker award.
Whether a tool such as optogenetics can be credited fairly with only three of six names.
statement.conflict_note: My profile documents shared work with Thomas Perlmann (a 2009 paper on stem-cell-derived dopamine neurons), with Sten Grillner and with Patrik Ernfors, none of whom are credited names on the shortlisted ballots. I am a circuit neuroscientist, so I flag that my field is nearest to B043 (optogenetics) and B047 (motor neuron disease); no recusal-level conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the preferred GLP-1 configuration.
